author: Vitor
notes: This was a nightmare to finish. I'm very proud to have achieved TLE here in ~45m, with 983 / 1040 testcases passed.
aiExplanation: This solution builds a **graph** where each node stores its character and a list of neighbours. For every `query`, the `collect` helper runs a **breadth-first search** from node `a` to node `b`, carrying along the string of characters collected so far, and returns that string as soon as `b` is reached (the input is a tree, so there is exactly one path). The `isPalindromic` helper then tracks how many characters occur an **odd** number of times; a string can be rearranged into a palindrome only when at most one character has an odd count, so it returns `odds <= 1`. An `update` query simply overwrites the character stored on the given node. Because each query rebuilds the entire path from scratch, the cost is **O(n) per query**, which is why this approach exceeded the time limit on large inputs.

author: Leetcode
notes: What even is all of this?
aiExplanation: This solution answers every query in roughly **logarithmic time** by combining three ideas. First, a DFS assigns each node an **Euler-tour interval** `[l[u], r[u]]` that covers the node and its whole subtree, and records ancestors at power-of-two distances so `lca` can find the **lowest common ancestor** of two nodes via binary lifting. Second, each letter is encoded as a single bit (`1 << (code - 97)`) and stored in a **Fenwick tree (BIT)** that combines values with XOR; by XOR-ing a node's bit across its subtree interval, `bit.query(l[u])` returns the XOR of all letters on the path from the root down to `u`. XOR behaves like a parity counter, so a bit is set exactly when that letter appears an **odd** number of times along the path. Third, for a `query u v`, the parity mask of the path is `query(l[u]) ^ query(l[v]) ^ bitOf(lca)`: the shared root-to-LCA segment cancels itself out and the LCA's own letter is added back once. The path can be rearranged into a palindrome when that mask has **at most one set bit**. An `update` XORs out the old letter's bit and XORs in the new one over the node's subtree range, keeping the tree consistent for later queries.
